title: Psalm 51 - Forgive Me Lord
speaker: Unknown Speaker
summary: This sermon explores Psalm 51 as David's prayer of repentance and confession following his sin with Bathsheba. The message emphasizes that forgiveness is grounded in God's mercy and grace rather than human merit, and addresses four groups: those who underestimate sin and grace, those who think the holy can't fall, those who believe the fallen can't rise, and those who think the forgiven become useless. The sermon calls believers to seek not only pardon but transformation through Christ's blood.

outline.title: The Occasion and Purpose of Psalm 51
subpoints: David wrote this psalm for corporate worship and public confession after his sin with Bathsheba

The psalm is written for four groups: those who underestimate sin and grace, those who think the holy cannot fall, those who believe the fallen cannot be restored, and those who think the forgiven are useless
Sin's consequences extend beyond the individual sinner to many others, as seen in David's family troubles
David willingly humiliated himself so others could learn from his example without repeating his mistakes

outline.title: The Basis of David's Appeal for Forgiveness (Verses 1-2)
subpoints: David appeals to God's loving-kindness, tender mercies, and covenant faithfulness, not his own merit or track record
He uses three terms for sin: transgression (willful defiance), iniquity (deviation from the right path), and sin (missing the divine mark)
He uses three terms for forgiveness: blot out (erase from record), wash (scrub clean like laundering), and cleanse (ceremonial purification)
David demonstrates true confession by making no excuses, offering no rationalizations, and refusing to shift blame

outline.title: The Vertical Orientation of Sin (Verses 3-4)
subpoints: Though David's sin affected many people, he recognizes it primarily as sin against God
Facing God's holiness, infinity, and immensity, all other aspects of sin fade by comparison
Only when we see sin against God in its true magnitude can we repent and confess to others
David's confession affirms God's right to judge and acknowledges that God owes him no forgiveness

outline.title: The Root Problem: A Sinful Nature (Verse 5)
subpoints: David traces his sin not to recent trauma or circumstance, but to his sinful nature from conception
We are sinners by nature who commit sins by practice, not sinners because we sin
The constitutional propensity to sin requires new life in Christ, not merely new habits
Only Jesus Christ is the exception to this universal sinfulness

outline.title: The Prayer for Cleansing and Power (Verses 7-12)
subpoints: David asks for ceremonial cleansing using hyssop imagery, which prefigures cleansing through Christ's blood and faith
He prays for spiritual power: a clean heart and steadfast spirit renewed within him
He prays for spiritual presence: restored intimacy and fellowship with God through His Holy Spirit
He prays for spiritual pleasure: the joy of salvation and the gladness that comes from God's presence
True repentance requires asking not only for pardon but for power to walk in future purity

outline.title: Three Applications for Modern Believers
subpoints: To the unsaved: Christ bore the condemnation sinners deserve; bring your guilt to Him through faith and repentance
To believers burdened by past sins: Christ's forgiveness is greater than your worst failure; do not carry the burden He has already borne
To all believers: pursue not only forgiveness but transformation; ask God to give you His Spirit's power for tomorrow's obedience
The gospel is not escape from judgment but becoming a new creation; the same grace that justifies also sanctifies

transcript:
## Psalm 51 - A Prayer of Repentance and Forgiveness

> "To the chief musician, a Psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet went to him after he had gone into Bathsheba. Have mercy upon me, O God, according to your loving kindness, according to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions. Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity and cleanse me from my sin, for I acknowledge my transgressions and my sin is always before me. Against you, you only have I sinned and done this evil in your sight that you may be found just when you speak and blameless when you judge. Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity and in sin my mother conceived me. Behold, you desire truth in inward parts and in the hidden part you will make me to know wisdom. Purge me with hyssop and I shall be clean. Wash me and I shall be whiter than snow. Make me hear joy and gladness that the bones you have broken may rejoice. Hide your face from my sins and blot out all my iniquities. Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me. Do not cast me away from your presence and do not take your Holy Spirit from me. Restore to me the joy of your salvation and uphold me by your generous spirit. Then I will teach transgressors your ways and sinners shall be converted to you. Deliver me from the guilt of blood, O God, the God of my salvation, and my tongue shall sing aloud of your righteousness. O Lord, open my lips and my mouth shall show forth your praise. For you do not desire sacrifice or else I would give it. You do not delight in burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit, a broken and a contrite heart. These, O God, you will not despise. Do good in your good pleasure to Zion. Build the walls of Jerusalem. Then you shall be pleased with the sacrifices of righteousness, with burnt offerings and whole burnt offering. Then they shall offer bowls on your altar." (Psalm 51)

In many ways, this is a preparatory sermon. We are in a regular Sunday series on 2 Corinthians, but this Sunday and next Sunday we will take a break from that series, and the Lord willing we will return to it on the ninth of August. Next Lord's Day, we will announce a disciplinary action taken by the church concerning one of our members. This psalm will prepare us for that, because the goal of church discipline is always forgiveness and reconciliation.

## The Four Groups Who Need This Psalm

I think this psalm has a special message for several groups of people.

### First: Those Who Misunderstand Sin and Grace

Psalm 51 is for those who have never come to grips with the horror of human sin and the magnitude of divine grace. Often, grace becomes meaningless and certainly less amazing because we lose sight of the depths of our depravity. When we do not have much to be forgiven, we do not think much of the grace of God or of God himself. David helps us on both counts by describing in this psalm in graphic detail the reality of his sin and the breathtaking glory of forgiving grace that we see in Jesus Christ.

### Second: Those Who Think No One Is Too Holy to Fall

This psalm is for those who think some people are too high or too holy to fall. Let us never forget that this psalm describes the experience of David, the king of Israel, the one who is called the man after God's own heart. No one is too high or too holy to fall. The apostle Paul in 2 Corinthians 10:12 says that we need to be careful, lest we fall.

### Third: Those Who Think the Fallen Cannot Rise

This psalm is for those who think that once you have fallen, you can never get back up again. There are several of us in that category, thinking that once we have fallen, we can never get back up again. It is for those who think it is possible to fall beyond the reach of God's grace and forgiveness or that there is a quantifiable limit to divine grace. Brothers and sisters, there is no limit to the grace of God. It is an attribute of God; therefore it is infinite, eternal, and unchangeable. No one is so holy that she cannot fall or that he cannot fall, and no one is so fallen that he or she cannot be forgiven by our Lord.

### Fourth: Those Who Think the Forgiven Become Useless

Psalm 51 is for those who think that if you have fallen and have actually gotten back up, perhaps even forgiven, you are still useless from that point on, both to God and to men. David's experience will prove otherwise. How many Psalms did David write after Psalm 51? There are a lot of them. Forgiveness brings alongside restoration and reconciliation.

All of us will fit in at least one of these groups, if not multiple. So take heed to what the Lord says to us here in this Psalm.

## The Historical Context and Purpose

The title of the Psalm is very helpful. It says, "To the chief musician, a Psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet went to him after he had gone into Bathsheba." It is proper to think that these titles are original to the Psalms. In every Hebrew manuscript, the original language in which the Psalm was written, the title is verse one. At least the copiers or the redactors of the book of Psalms believed that was original to the title, and I think that is true. This is the inspired description of the occasion of the Psalm, what led David to write it. If you want to read about the historical setting of the Psalm, you can look at 2 Samuel, starting at chapter 11.

None of us like to have our struggles and problems broadcast publicly, much less our sins of the flesh. Yet here, we are told that this Psalm was written to the chief musician, by the sinner himself. How would you like if we projected all your sins to music for all of us to sing about your sin? That is what Psalm 51 is. It was written for the corporate worship of the church so that David's sin would be known.

This Psalm is remarkable and in many ways unparalleled as a description of the nature of conviction, confession, and forgiveness. David did not care how many people knew his sin, as long as God forgave him. That was his conviction. That was his desire. That was his confession.

## The Far-Reaching Consequences of Sin

By the same time that we celebrate with David the joy of having one sin washed clean, we do not forget that his transgressions reaped significant and far-reaching consequences. David put this to writing so that you and I can be warned that though we are forgiven, our sins impact more people and situations than we might expect.

In 2 Samuel 12, Nathan comes with a denunciation and accusation. He tells a story: there is a wealthy farmer with a whole flock of lambs. Someone comes to visit him and he goes next door to a guy who had just one little lamb. He grabs that lamb, kills it, and serves it to the visitors. David becomes indignant and says the man must die. Then Nathan says to David, "You are the man." You are the woman who sinned against God.

This sin brought great devastation in David's own family. The baby that he had conceived with Bathsheba died. There is trouble with Amnon in the rape of his sister Tamar, and Amnon ends up dying. There is trouble with Absalom, who rebels against his father. For about five chapters, we read about that struggle, and Absalom ends up dying. Trouble and affairs in the state from that moment on—rebellion from within and rebellion from without—all directly related to this sin of David. Ultimately even a son dies when Adonijah attempts to usurp the throne when Solomon comes to power.

The lesson is that while sin is certainly personal, in many cases it is anything but private. That is one of the reasons why David is willing to humiliate himself and have the church now for three thousand years reading and singing his very sins—so that you and I do not have to go through it. That is what David is saying to us here. Learn from me.

## The Basis of David's Appeal for Forgiveness

### Verses 1-2: Appeal to God's Mercy, Not Merit

David asks for forgiveness for his sins, but on what basis does David ask for forgiveness? Look at verses 1 and 2:

> "Have mercy upon me, O God, according to your loving kindness, according to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions. Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity and cleanse me from my sin."

Does David appeal to his track record as king of Israel as the basis on which God should grant him forgiveness? Does he remind God of how many psalms he has written and how much of a blessing they have been to God's children? Does he cite his faithful service or parade a long list of character witnesses that can attest to how great a guy he is? No, he does not do any of those things. He does not expect to be forgiven based on his sincerity. He does not expect to be forgiven based on his spiritual intensity or deep pain for having sinned or fervor of heart or promise not to sin again or his depth of determination to somehow make up to God. None of these things are the basis on which David says, "God, forgive me."

Now, that is not to say sincerity and zeal and conviction are not important, but David's appeal is based on what he knows of God's mercy and compassion and loving kindness, His covenant faithfulness.

### The Three Words for Sin

Noticing verses one and two, David uses three words to describe his sin. This indicates on his part an acknowledgement that it is sin and not just some trivial mistake. He calls it a transgression—a willful, self-assertive defiance of God. He calls it an iniquity—a deviation from the right path. And he calls it a sin—a missing of the divine mark.

David wants God to know and wants us all to know that he is not saying that he committed an indiscretion. He uses every word possible for sin to let God know and us know that he is not trying to make excuses, that he understands he broke God's law, that he understands he broke fellowship with God, and yet he knows that even then he can trust in God's loving kindness, grace, and compassion to forgive him. And that is how he comes to the Savior.

### The Three Words for Forgiveness

Equally vivid are the three words he uses in his plea for forgiveness. He asks God to blot out his transgressions—to erase it from the record or wipe it away. In television shows about court of law, a lawyer says something and the judge says, "Strike it from the record." And yet God does that in forgiveness. He strikes our sin from the record and He actively does not remember and bring that up against us.

David asks God to blot out his transgressions. But also he begs God to wash him from his sin in verse 2 and verse 7. This word is often used of a woman first saturating a garment with soap and then treading it underfoot on a rock, beating and pummeling it as rushing waters pour over it. One can almost hear David cheerfully praying, "Gracious Lord, do that to my spirit. My sin is like a deep dye stain that has soiled the fabric of my soul and no ordinary soap or detergent, far less any good works I might perform, can remove it. My transgressions are like ground in dirt. Lord, scrub me clean by your mercy and your grace."

Finally, David uses the word cleanse. This word was used for ceremonial purification in the Old Testament. Just make me clean. I cannot do it. But you can.

## The Magnitude of Sin's Offense

### Verses 3-4: A Confession Without Excuse

When David turns to confess the magnitude of his sin, his language is no less graphic:

> "For I acknowledge my transgressions and my sins are always before me. Against you, you only have I sinned and done this evil in your sight that you may be found just when you speak and blameless when you judge."

Do you see what David is not doing here? David makes no excuses. He does not offer any rationalization. He refuses to shift blame in his confession. He does not say, "Well, wait a minute, God. Yes, I sinned. I admit that. But it takes two to tangle. What about Bathsheba's complicity in all this? She is so beautiful and seductive. Besides, the pressures of being king over your people are enormous. Given what I faced on a daily basis, I would expect you to cut me some slack here."

And yet he does not do that. How often do we do that? Brothers and sisters, the moment we add a "but" in our confession, we are not confessing at all. We are just rationalizing why our sin is not really sin, or we are rationalizing that somebody else might be worse than us.

There is an impulse with parents, right? As long as there is one more misbehaved kid in the church than yours, you are okay, right? At least our kid is not as bad. And often that is how we approach sin. "At least I am not as bad as..." And yet, brothers and sisters, the widest lie, the simplest sin, would have been enough to nail the Son of God to the cross because of the infinite chasm, the separation it creates between us and the Holy God of Scripture.

David makes no excuses. There is no insanity plea or appeal to diminish capacity. He says, "My sin is always before me." It is not intermittent but a perpetual obsession, a sight from which he can never turn away. It is as if seared on the inside of his eyelids. He sees it all the time.

### The Vertical Orientation: Sin Against God

David says that his sin is ultimately against God alone. You might say, "Wait, what? God alone? Well, I think Uriah would have something to say about that. He is dead. Bathsheba is brought into the king's harm. The baby died. The nation of Israel has been sinned against. And yet David stands here and says against God and God only, I have sinned. How can it be?"

A commentator suggests that face to face with God, he sees nothing else. No one else. He can think of nothing else but His presence forgotten, His holiness outraged, His love scorned. Just the thought that his fellowship with God had been severed made David not see anything else. This is it. This is the most important orientation—the vertical orientation. I sin against you. It is not a dismissal of anything else, but compared to our sin against God, everything else is nothing.

Yet brothers and sisters, we tend to be more upset about sins against us than sins against God. We tend to be more upset about commandments five through ten than we are upset about when commandments one through four are broken. Brothers and sisters, you have to come to a place where when we see our sin against God, we see God in His true holiness, His true immensity and infinity, and everything else just pales in comparison.

It is when we see sin in that way that we are actually able to repent to others. Because wherever we have humbled ourselves before God, humbling ourselves before other people is nothing. David is so broken that he has treated God with such disregard that he is blinded to all other aspects or objects of his behavior because his concern is with God.

David's confession is not simply to get things off his chest as if confession were merely therapeutic release. His confession is designed to tell everyone that God was right all along, that God's judgment was true, just, and God is blameless. In verse 4 he says, "You have all the right to judge me. You do not owe me forgiveness. And if you choose not to forgive me, I will still love you." That is what David is saying here. You are still God. You are still the one. I do not say this because you owe me any forgiveness.

## The Root Problem: Sinful Nature

### Verse 5: Born in Sin

> "Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity and in sin, my mother conceived me."

How long has David had this problem with sin? Did his problem start at two when the terrible twos came along? Did it start at puberty or at twelve? Or on that infamous birthday where the suffix "teen" is attached to their name? Is that when David's problem began? Was he turned to the dark side by some childhood or teenage trauma?

The problem, David says, is not so much that he sins. The problem is that he is sinful and always has been. David says, "These deeds of the flesh are symptomatic of a much deeper problem. The fact is, I was brought forth in iniquity and in sin, my mother conceived me. My transgressions are not of recent vintage. This was no freak one-off event. I have been a sinner from my mother's womb."

And there is only one exception to that. And that is not you. It is the Lord Jesus Christ.

We are not sinners because we sin. We sin because we are sinners. David confesses his sinful nature in verse 5 as the root cause of his actual sins in verse 4. But he makes no effort to excuse himself on that basis. In other words, David's problem—and yours too—is not that we commit individual acts of sin. The problem is that we have a constitutional propensity to sin. What we need most is not a new lifestyle. What we need most is new life in Christ. Not new habits, but a new heart.

## The Prayer for Cleansing and Transformation

### Verses 7-12: Three Dimensions of Prayer

What hope is there for this? Countless Christians feel spiritually paralyzed by the lingering stain of sin. Neither therapy nor religious formulas nor good intentions or good deeds can erase the vivid memory of their transgressions or bring cleansing to the defining sense of guilt. The oppressive weight of their failures is virtually suffocating them.

What do we do then? How do we take this burden off? Is there anyone who would be willing to take this burden from me?

> "If we confess our sins, He, God, is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (1 John 1:8-9)

Psalm 51 is a refreshing and heartwarming reminder of the hope of forgiveness. But it is even more than that. David not only prays for pardon from past sins but also for power to walk in future purity. He makes an impassioned plea for ceremonial cleansing.

### The Hyssop and Cleansing

In verse 7 he says, "Purge me with hyssop and I shall be clean." David's choice of word is very instructive here. Hyssop is an aromatic herb with a straight stalk and a bushy head, somewhere between a cilantro bunch and a broccoli stalk. It was dipped in the blood of the sacrifice and then sprinkled seven times on the persons who were defiled. You can read about that in Leviticus 14 and Numbers 19. The word here translated "purge" might more literally be rendered "de-sin me."

Only then would David be clean and whiter than snow. Can this actually happen to sinners like you and me? Can we be de-sinned? Can we be cleansed? Yes. But not through the blood of bulls and goats, but through the blood of Christ sprinkled on us by faith. Faith is a hyssop, as it were, of forgiveness.

### Joy and Restoration (Verse 8)

But David longs for more. In verse 8 he says:

> "Make me hear joy and gladness that the bones you have broken may rejoice."

The things that God would enable him to hear joy and gladness. Make me to experience the joy and gladness that come from hearing the announcement of forgiveness. He may even have in mind a priestly or prophetic oracle in which another loudly declares that his sins are forgiven.

Brothers and sisters, sin can be as spiritually devastating and painful to the soul as broken bones are to the body. David cries out that the bones you have broken may rejoice. Why is David ultimately in so much pain? Sure, he has sinned. But what is the ultimate cause? Who broke his bones? God did. God brought the pain so that David would see his need of God.

Some of you are going through a lot of pain right now. Do not waste the pain that God has brought into your life by not turning to Christ and seeing Him in His beauty, the satisfaction and the healing of all the pain that is in your heart.

### Blotting Out and Forgetting (Verse 9)

David desires that his entire being, body and soul, might once again celebrate and rejoice in the blessedness of communion with God. Once more he prays:

> "Hide your face from my sins. Blot out all my iniquities."

He says, "Do not look any longer at my failures. Let not your eyes gaze on my weakness. Blot it from view. Erase it from memory." And the Lord says, "As far as the east is from the west, I have removed the guilt of your sins from you." How far is the east from the west? Can you get any closer to the east by going west? Or can you get any closer to the west by going east? The idea is that they never meet. That is what God has done for you who have repented of your sins in Jesus Christ.

### Spiritual Power, Presence, and Pleasure (Verses 10-12)

With verses 10 and 12, David's prayer gets even more specific. In verse 10, he prays, Lord, give me spiritual power. In verse 11, Lord, give me spiritual presence. In verse 12, Lord, give me spiritual pleasure.

> "Do not cast me away from your presence and do not take your Holy Spirit from me. Restore to me the joy of your salvation. Uphold me by your generous spirit. Then I will teach transgressors your ways, and sinners shall be converted to you."

What David is saying here is that simply asking for pardon is not enough. One must also ask for the power by which not to commit the same sin again. It is not just mere makeover. Remember the show Extreme Makeover Home Edition? In the beginning, they would come and remodel one room. But as the show progressed, all of a sudden they were taking the house down to the foundation and rebuilding the whole house. That is what God wants. That is not a makeover. No matter how extreme. David refuses to settle for a glossing over of his faults and pleads for a replacement of the old with the new.

He wants a clean heart. He wants a right spirit—steadfast, firm, reliable spirit—which is his way of describing the inner core and the center of his life. This is what is essential for a life of holiness.

David cannot bear the thought of the loss of intimacy, of fellowship, and its accompanying joys. So he prays that he not be cast from God's presence or suffer the loss of God's spirit. It is not that David has lost his salvation. It is not that the Spirit's regenerating power has left him, but the joy of the presence of the Spirit is gone. And he wants that back. He is not willing to find that in substitutes like work, drugs, sex, and the other things that appeal to our senses. He wants the joy to come from a renewed feeling of the presence of the Spirit in his heart.

## Three Applications for Today

### Application One: To Those Who Have Never Trusted Christ

To those who have never trusted Christ, bring your guilt to the only one who can remove it. David understood that no amount of good works, no amount of religious activity, no amount of sincere remorse could erase the guilt of sin. We cannot erase it ourselves. It did not work for David. It does not work for us. We may hide our sin from other people, but we can never hide our sin from God.

The good news of the gospel is that Jesus Christ came to save sinners. So if you are perfect, you have no hope. But if you know the darkness of your heart, praise the Lord, you are right to be saved. You are welcome, for Christ has come for those who know that they are guilty.

If you have never repented and believed in Christ, today is God's invitation to come. Christ bore the condemnation that sinners deserve so that everyone who trusts in Him may be washed, justified, and welcomed into God's family. In the words of the prophet Isaiah:

> "Though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow." (Isaiah 1:18)

### Application Two: To Believers Burdened by Past Sins

To believers burdened by past sins, know this: Christ's forgiveness is greater than your worst failure. Christ's forgiveness is greater than your worst failure. Some Christians continue to live as though their greatest sin has the final word. But David teaches us otherwise. His adultery and murder did not become the defining chapter of his life because God's grace wrote the final chapter of his life.

Forgiveness does not erase every earthly consequence of sin, but it does remove its eternal condemnation. If you have confessed your sins to Christ, do not continue carrying the burden.

Do you remember when Christian let the burden go in Pilgrim's Progress? Almost to the end of his journey. Do you know when you are supposed to let your burden go? At that very moment—when you come to faith in Christ. At the very moment you repent and receive God's forgiveness, the burden is gone. The chains fall off. It is gone.

So if you have confessed your sins to Christ, do not continue carrying a burden. He has already borne it for you. The blood of Jesus cleanses completely. So live not in the presence of remembered guilt, but in the freedom of forgiving grace.

### Application Three: To Every Believer

And lastly, to every believer, pursue not only forgiveness but transformation. David did not stop with "Forgive me." He prayed, "Create in me a clean heart." The Gospel is not only about escaping judgment, it is about becoming a new creation. Christ not only pardoned sinners, He changes them.

Ask God not only to forgive yesterday's sins, but to give you His Spirit's power for tomorrow's obedience. The same grace that justifies also sanctifies. The Savior who washes you clean is also committed to making you holy.

So brothers and sisters, make your daily prayer become like David's prayer:

> "Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me."

Let that be your cry. That is the Gospel. That is the hope of forgiveness and transformation. That is the hope of Jesus Christ.
